pedagogy.summary:
- **Age:** 5–7 years (KS1)

- **Topic:** How Breathing Works — we breathe air into our lungs through the nose and mouth; lungs take in oxygen (which the body needs to live) and we breathe out carbon dioxide as waste

- **Standards — UK (DfE KS1, Animals including humans):** statutory KS1 content is the basic needs for survival — water, food and AIR; the detailed respiratory system (trachea, alveoli, gas exchange) is Y5/Y6+ and KS3. So at KS1 this is the age-appropriate 'why we need air' encounter that seeds later respiratory study.

- **Standards — US (NGSS):** nearest is K-LS1-1 (what animals need to survive, including air); the respiratory system as an interacting subsystem is formalised at MS-LS1-3. Enrichment on both sides at this age.

- **Operational details:** Build on what the child already does thousands of times a day but never notices. Three ideas: (1) the AIR PATH — air goes in through the nose/mouth, down the windpipe, into the two lungs in the chest; (2) the WHY — air contains oxygen, and the body needs oxygen to stay alive (that's why you can't hold your breath forever); (3) the WASTE — the body makes carbon dioxide, which we breathe OUT. Make it embodied: put hands on the ribs/chest and feel it rise and fall; take a deep breath and feel the lungs fill; breathe on a cold mirror/window to 'see' the warm, moist air you breathe out. The key conceptual correction: we breathe IN and OUT the SAME air (a mixture), not 'pure oxygen in, pure carbon dioxide out' — the lungs just TAKE SOME oxygen from the air and ADD some carbon dioxide. Also correct the location: lungs are in the chest (two of them), not the belly, and breathing is not the same as the stomach/eating. Keep the diaphragm mechanism for Y5/6 — at KS1, 'your chest gets bigger to pull air in' is enough.

- **Checkpoint:** Tier A (concrete, embodied). Success = trace air nose/mouth → windpipe → lungs, state that lungs take oxygen from air that the body needs, and state that we breathe out carbon dioxide as waste. Depth stops at path + oxygen-in + carbon-dioxide-out.
bestPractices: Start from the child's own body — hands on ribs to feel the chest rise and fall, a deep breath to feel the lungs fill — so breathing becomes noticed, not abstract.
Use the cold-mirror trick (breathe out onto glass to see the moist warm air) to make invisible exhaled air real and evidence the 'we breathe something out'.
Correct the 'pure oxygen in / pure carbon dioxide out' myth: we breathe the same air mixture in and out; lungs just take some oxygen and add some carbon dioxide.
Locate the two lungs correctly in the chest (not the belly) and keep breathing distinct from eating/the stomach.
Tie the WHY to a felt limit — you can't hold your breath forever because the body must keep getting oxygen — making the need visceral.
Keep the diaphragm mechanism for Y5/6; at KS1 'the chest gets bigger to pull air in' is the right grain.
keyRepresentations: Hands-on-ribs feeling the chest rise (in) and fall (out)
A simple air-path diagram: nose/mouth → windpipe → two lungs
The cold-mirror/window fogging up to show exhaled moist air
A balloon-in-chest image for lungs filling and emptying (with the limit that lungs aren't hollow balloons)
An 'air is a mixture' picture: some oxygen taken out, some carbon dioxide added
commonMisconceptions: Thinking we breathe in pure oxygen and breathe out pure carbon dioxide, rather than the same air mixture with some oxygen removed and carbon dioxide added.
Believing air/breath goes into the stomach or belly rather than the lungs in the chest.
Thinking there is one lung, or not knowing lungs are in the chest.
Confusing breathing (air in/out) with eating/drinking, or thinking the windpipe and food pipe are the same tube.
Believing you breathe out ALL the oxygen, or that exhaled air has no oxygen left in it.
Thinking breathing is optional/voluntary only, not understanding the body needs a constant oxygen supply.

learn.summary: KS1 (ages 5–7) first encounter with how breathing works: air enters through the nose/mouth, travels down the windpipe to the two lungs in the chest; the lungs take some oxygen (which the body needs to stay alive) from the air and add carbon dioxide (waste) to the breath we send back out. The core conceptual target is that the SAME air mixture goes in and out — changed, not swapped for pure gases — plus correct lung location (chest, not belly) and a felt reason we must keep breathing. Keep the diaphragm mechanism for later years; at KS1 'the chest gets bigger to pull air in' is the right grain. Activities centre on the child's own body and an animated, driveable breath model, with recognition checks kept as lighter scaffolds.

activities.title: Breathe with me: drive your own breath and watch the air change
feedback: If a learner says the out-breath is identical to the in-breath, point to the dots: some oxygen stayed in the body and carbon dioxide was added — ask why we'd keep breathing if nothing changed.
If a learner thinks all the oxygen is removed, show that oxygen dots still remain in the outgoing air — the lungs take only some.
When the hold-your-breath meter fills, connect it to the real feeling of being out of breath after running: the body can't stop needing oxygen.
activities.rationale: Breathing is an automatic, invisible process the child performs constantly but never notices; an embodied, driveable model lets them work the breath and make the oxygen-taken/carbon-dioxide-added exchange visible. The coloured-air moment targets the central KS1 misconception that we breathe pure oxygen in and pure carbon dioxide out, and the hold-your-breath meter grounds the DfE basic-need-for-air idea in a felt reason the body must keep getting oxygen. Pairing on-screen action with hands on the ribs ties the model to the real rise and fall of the chest. The oxygen-dots, carbon-dioxide-dots and hold-your-breath meter are illustrative design examples, not required mechanisms — a paper flip-sequence or acted-out breath could carry the same insight; comparative effectiveness is untested.
sourceClaims: Inhaled and exhaled air are both mixtures; the lungs take up some oxygen and release carbon dioxide, so exhaled air still contains oxygen — it is not 'pure carbon dioxide'.
DfE KS1 statutory content includes the basic needs of animals including humans for survival (water, food and AIR); detailed respiratory anatomy and gas exchange come later (Y5/Y6 and KS3).
learnerActions: Put one hand on your ribs/chest and take a slow deep breath in, then let it out, feeling the chest rise and fall.
Using an animated model, tap-and-hold to breathe IN: watch the chest widen and a stream of air carrying oxygen dots flow in through the nose/mouth, down the windpipe, and puff up the two lungs.
Release to breathe OUT and watch the air leave: notice that some oxygen dots stayed behind in the body and new carbon-dioxide dots have joined the outgoing breath.
Say in your own words what changed about the air between going in and coming out.
Watch a 'hold your breath' meter climb until the body insists on a breath, and connect this to why air must keep coming.
activities.intendedInsight: Breathing is a repeating in/out process: the SAME air goes in and out but is changed — the lungs take some oxygen (which the body needs to live) and add carbon-dioxide waste. We can't stop breathing because the body keeps needing oxygen.

activities.title: See your warm breath on cold glass
feedback: If a learner says breathing out is 'just pushing the same air', point to the fog: the out-breath is warm and moist from inside you, so it has been changed.
Reinforce that the fog is water the body added, part of how the out-breath differs from the in-breath.
activities.rationale: The cold-mirror trick makes invisible exhaled air observable and gives concrete evidence for 'we breathe something out', supporting the in-changed-out picture. It uses everyday materials and needs no screen.
sourceClaims: Inhaled and exhaled air are both mixtures; the lungs take up some oxygen and release carbon dioxide, so exhaled air still contains oxygen — it is not 'pure carbon dioxide'.
learnerActions: Take a deep breath and breathe out slowly with an open mouth ('haaa') onto a cold mirror or window.
Look at the fog that appears and feel that the breath is warm and moist.
Say what this shows: we really do breathe something out, and it is different from ordinary room air.
activities.intendedInsight: Exhaled air is real and carries moisture and warmth from inside the body — evidence that we breathe something out, not nothing, and that the out-breath differs from the in-breath.

activities.title: Trace the air path and find your lungs
feedback: If a learner says the air goes to the tummy/stomach, trace the windpipe to the lungs and note the food pipe is a separate tube; use hands on the chest to feel the lungs expand.

If a child notices their tummy moving during a big breath, acknowledge that the belly can be felt to move, but the air itself travels to the lungs in the chest — the deeper reason for the belly movement (the diaphragm) is for later years.
If a learner says there is one lung, show there are two, both in the chest.
If a learner says exhaled air has no oxygen, reveal that only some oxygen is taken out.
activities.rationale: A tap-to-reveal chest illustration is effective for the air path and lung location and for addressing the belly-breathing and pure-gas myths. It is offered here as a scaffold: static or lift-the-flap art does not itself show the in/out cycle or the ongoing oxygen/CO2 exchange, so it supports but does not replace the driveable breath work.
sourceClaims: Inhaled and exhaled air are both mixtures; the lungs take up some oxygen and release carbon dioxide, so exhaled air still contains oxygen — it is not 'pure carbon dioxide'.
learnerActions: On a chest illustration, tap nose/mouth → windpipe → the two lungs to trace where air goes.

Put hands on your tummy and on your chest, take a big breath, and decide where the air actually goes inside you — then check that the air travels to the lungs in the chest, not into the belly or stomach.

Answer a lift-the-flap question: 'Do our lungs take ALL the oxygen out of the air?' → reveal 'No — they take just some, so the air we breathe out still has oxygen in it, and carbon dioxide has been added.'
Place the lungs correctly: a myth-buster flap shows two lungs in the chest, not one, and not in the belly.
activities.intendedInsight: Air travels nose/mouth → windpipe → two lungs in the chest; breathing is separate from the stomach/eating, and the out-breath still contains some oxygen.

activities.title: Quick checks: order the path and name the waste
feedback: For a wrong ordering, re-trace the path with the child from the nose down to the lungs.
If carbon dioxide is missed, remind that it is the waste the body adds and sends out.
For the lung-location item, confirm the lungs are in the chest, not the belly.
activities.rationale: Short recognition items can confirm the air-path and in/out facts. Recognition responses do not by themselves elicit independent construction or show the in/out cycle, so these items are a light confirmation layer, not the main embodied first encounter for this age.
learnerActions: Put the air path in order: nose → windpipe → lungs.
Choose what we breathe out as waste (carbon dioxide).
Decide true or false: 'The lungs are in the chest.'
activities.intendedInsight: Recall the air path, the location of the lungs, and that carbon dioxide is the waste we breathe out.

activities.title: Talk it through with friendly lungs
feedback: If the learner can't say why breathing can't stop, link it to the hold-your-breath feeling: the body keeps needing oxygen.
Prompt the learner to mention the warm, moist breath they saw on the glass as evidence something is breathed out.
activities.rationale: A talking-lungs dialogue can engage the child and prompt them to articulate reasoning. At 5–7 the understanding is built mainly by feeling and doing the breath, so discussion works best paired with the hands-on and mirror activities rather than on its own.
learnerActions: Respond to a friendly-lungs character that asks you to take a deep breath and breathe out slowly with an open mouth ('haaa') onto a cold mirror.
Explain to the character what you just saw and felt.
Answer the character's question: 'Why can't I stop breathing?'
activities.intendedInsight: Putting the experience into words — what was seen, felt, and why the body needs air — consolidates the idea that the body must keep getting oxygen.

constraints: KS1 depth stops at: trace air nose/mouth → windpipe → lungs; lungs take some oxygen the body needs; we breathe out carbon dioxide as waste. Do not teach trachea/alveoli detail, gas-exchange mechanism, or the diaphragm — reserve these for Y5/Y6+ and KS3.
At KS1, 'the chest gets bigger to pull air in' is the right explanation; keep the diaphragm implicit.

Core correction: we breathe the same air mixture in and out — the lungs take SOME oxygen and add some carbon dioxide; exhaled air still contains oxygen. Avoid 'pure oxygen in, pure carbon dioxide out'.

Locate the two lungs in the chest (not the belly) and keep breathing distinct from eating/the stomach; the windpipe is a separate tube from the food pipe. The air we breathe in goes to the lungs, not into the stomach/belly — though the belly may be felt to move, which is a diaphragm effect reserved for later years.
The balloon-in-chest image is an approximation only: lungs are not hollow balloons — flag this limit if the image is used.
Recognition items confirm facts but do not themselves show independent construction or the in/out cycle; use them as a secondary check, not the primary first encounter.

Oxygen dots, carbon-dioxide dots, the hold-your-breath meter, lift-the-flap reveals and the coloured-air animation are optional illustrative examples of the learning mechanism, not mandatory features; their comparative efficacy is untested.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. All activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.
Two of the three cited sources (NGSS and British Lung Foundation / Asthma + Lung UK) are marked verified:false in the source row; treat their claims as unconfirmed.

The source frames a 3D lung model as adding 'no conceptual gain' for KS1. Softened here: a 3D model is simply not needed for this particular path + oxygen-in + CO2-out objective at this age; no universal claim about 3D ineffectiveness is made.

The source's strong claim that the coloured-air animation 'quietly kills' or is uniquely able to defeat the misconception is softened — an animated exchange is one effective approach among several (paper sequences, acted breaths, mirror evidence); comparative necessity is not established by the available sources.

In the 'find your lungs' activity, a child's belly may visibly move during a deep breath; this is a diaphragm effect reserved for Y5/6 and does NOT mean air enters the stomach. The KS1 teaching point — air travels to the lungs in the chest, not into the belly/stomach — remains correct; the prompt asks where the air goes, and the activity feedback now acknowledges the belly movement rather than implying the belly stays completely still.

Checked air-path and physiology statements for internal consistency: exhaled air still containing some oxygen, two lungs in the chest, and 'same air changed' are consistent across pedagogy, assessment and sources; no arithmetic or force/motion content to audit here.

probeDeeper: Put one hand on your tummy and one on your chest and take a big breath — which one fills with air? Where did it really go?
If air just went in and came straight back out the same, why would we need to keep breathing all the time?
You breathe out carbon dioxide — where in your body do you think that came from?
assess.correctAnswer: The air goes down the windpipe into the lungs (not the tummy). The body wants it because the lungs take OXYGEN out of the air, and the body needs oxygen to stay alive. The air breathed out is different — it has less oxygen and more carbon dioxide, which the body doesn't need — so breathing out gets rid of waste carbon dioxide.

errorPatterns.pattern: Breathed-in and breathed-out air are the same — you just push the same air back out unchanged.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Establish that the body keeps some oxygen and adds carbon dioxide — so out-air differs; ask why we'd need to keep breathing if nothing changed.
errorPatterns.distractor: It's exactly the same air going straight back out.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Says the out-breath is identical to the in-breath; nothing is taken from the air.

errorPatterns.pattern: Air goes into the stomach / fills your tummy.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Trace the windpipe to the lungs (a separate tube from the one food takes); use hands on chest to feel the lungs, not the tummy, expand.
errorPatterns.distractor: The air goes down into my tummy.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Names the tummy or stomach as where the air goes.

errorPatterns.pattern: We breathe just to move the chest / breathing isn't for getting something the body needs.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Link breathing to staying alive — the lungs take oxygen the whole body needs; connect to feeling out of breath after running.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Describes breathing with no mention of oxygen or a bodily need for it.

responseLevels.gap: Thinks air goes to the tummy, or that in-air and out-air are identical; no sense the body takes something from the air.
responseLevels.full: Traces air to the lungs, states the body takes oxygen it needs to live, and explains the out-breath differs (less oxygen, more carbon-dioxide waste) — a coherent in-changed-out picture.
responseLevels.partial: Knows air goes to the lungs and mentions oxygen, but treats the out-breath as the same air, or can't say what changed or why the body needs it.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: When you take a big breath in, where does the air actually go inside you, and why does your body want it? And is the air you breathe out exactly the same as the air you breathed in, or different — and how?
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child who thinks air fills the tummy, or that in-air and out-air are the same, reveals the naive model. A child who understands says air goes to the lungs, the body takes the oxygen it needs, and the out-breath carries waste carbon dioxide. The tier-two 'same or different' forces the change to be named, which the naive 'just push the air back out' idea cannot do.
